steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper examining temporal concept drift in stance detection towards COVID-19 vaccination on Twitter. Motivate the problem, explain temporal concept drift and where it has been studied, state the gap and our research questions, and summarise what we do.

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
The COVID-19 pandemic had a big impact on global health and caused considerable social and economic disruption. Promoting vaccination has been recognised statistically as a vital tactic for curbing the spread of the COVID-19 virus and reducing the burden on healthcare systems. But attitudes towards COVID-19 vaccination have varied, and some people have expressed hesitation and resistance. These concerns come from factors like side effects, conspiracy theories and distrust of healthcare authorities. To promote vaccine uptake it is important to understand, on a large scale, what contributes to hesitant or negative attitudes towards COVID-19 vaccination. Recently there has been growing interest in using supervised machine learning to automatically detect the stance of users towards COVID-19 vaccination on social media.

Temporal concept drift is the phenomenon in NLP where the statistical properties of a dataset, such as the distribution of topics, change over time. It is especially relevant in applications where the data is collected over long periods, like financial forecasting or tasks based on social media data. It can also make model performance degrade because the textual content in a static dataset varies over time. The impact of temporal concept drift has been studied in several domains, including topic classification, rumour detection, gender equality, and hate speech detection. Also, previous work evaluated how different factors of datasets and models affect performance over time in different classification tasks.

However, nobody has studied temporal aspects in stance detection about COVID-19 vaccination. And the underlying distribution of users' stances may change over time because of things like evolving political agendas and new viral variants, so the temporal factor needs to be taken into account.

- This study: temporal concept drift in COVID-19 vaccine stance detection on Twitter, first time
  - Q1 significant effect, as in other domains (rumour, legal, biomedical)?
  - Q2 performance across multiple languages?
  - Q3 domain adaptation to mitigate drift?
  - Q4 semantic variation train vs test -> degradation or improvement?
- What we do
  - (i) five public monolingual + multilingual datasets
  - (ii) controlled experiments, transformer-based PLMs, chronological vs random splits
  - (iii) correlation tests: performance vs disparity between training and test sets (positive/negative)

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
The COVID-19 pandemic had a big impact on global health and caused considerable social and economic disruption. Promoting vaccination has been recognised statistically as a vital tactic for curbing the spread of the COVID-19 virus and reducing the burden on healthcare systems. But attitudes towards COVID-19 vaccination have varied, and some people have expressed hesitation and resistance. These concerns come from factors like side effects, conspiracy theories and distrust of healthcare authorities. To promote vaccine uptake it is important to understand, on a large scale, what contributes to hesitant or negative attitudes towards COVID-19 vaccination. Recently there has been growing interest in using supervised machine learning to automatically detect the stance of users towards COVID-19 vaccination on social media.

Temporal concept drift is the phenomenon in NLP where the statistical properties of a dataset, such as the distribution of topics, change over time. It is especially relevant in applications where the data is collected over long periods, like financial forecasting or tasks based on social media data. It can also make model performance degrade because the textual content in a static dataset varies over time. The impact of temporal concept drift has been studied in several domains, including topic classification, rumour detection, gender equality, and hate speech detection. Also, previous work evaluated how different factors of datasets and models affect performance over time in different classification tasks.

However, nobody has studied temporal aspects in stance detection about COVID-19 vaccination. And the underlying distribution of users' stances may change over time because of things like evolving political agendas and new viral variants, so the temporal factor needs to be taken into account.

In this study we examine temporal concept drift in stance detection towards COVID-19 vaccination on Twitter for the first time. We focus on these research questions:

- Q1: Does temporal concept drift have a significant effect on COVID-19 vaccine stance detection, like it does in other domains (e.g., rumour, legal, biomedical, etc.)?

- Q2: How does the performance of the model differ across multiple languages?

- Q3: Can domain adaptation approaches be used to mitigate the impact of temporal concept drift on stance classification?

- Q4: Does semantic variation between the training and test sets make the predictive performance of the model worse or better?

For this we (i) evaluate five publicly available monolingual and multilingual datasets, (ii) run a set of controlled experiments where we evaluate different transformer-based pretrained language models (PLMs) with chronological and random splits and (iii) do correlation tests to look at the relationship (i.e., positive or negative) between the predictive performance of the model and the disparity between the two subsets (i.e., training and test sets).

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
The COVID-19 pandemic has had a profound impact on global health and has caused considerable social and economic disruption [1]. Promoting vaccination has been statistically recognised as a vital tactic for curbing the spread of the COVID-19 virus and reducing the burden on healthcare systems [2]. However, attitudes towards COVID-19 vaccination have varied, with some individuals expressing hesitation and resistance [3,4]. These concerns are caused by factors including side effects, conspiracy theories, and distrust of healthcare authorities [5]. To promote vaccine uptake, it is important to understand on a large scale the factors that contribute to hesitant or negative attitudes towards COVID-19 vaccination [6]. Recently, there has been growing interest in using supervised machine learning approaches to automatically detect users' stance towards COVID-19 vaccination on social media [7,8,9].

Temporal concept drift refers to the phenomenon in NLP where the statistical properties of a dataset, such as the distribution of topics, change over time [10]. It is particularly relevant in applications where data is collected over extended periods, such as financial forecasting or tasks based on social media data [11,12,13]. It can also degrade model performance due to the temporal variation of textual content in a static dataset [14,15]. The impact of temporal concept drift has been investigated in several domains, including topic classification [16], rumour detection [14], gender equality [17], and hate speech detection [18,19]. Moreover, [12] evaluated how different factors of datasets and models affect performance over time across different classification tasks.

However, temporal aspects have not been studied in stance detection concerning COVID-19 vaccination. Furthermore, the underlying distribution of users' stances may change over time due to factors such as evolving political agendas and emerging viral variants, which makes it necessary to take the temporal factor into account.

This study examines temporal concept drift in stance detection towards COVID-19 vaccination on Twitter for the first time. Specifically, we focus on the following research questions:

- • Q1: Does temporal concept drift have a significant effect on COVID-19 vaccine stance detection, as previously seen in other domains (e.g., rumour, legal, biomedical, etc.)?

- • Q2: How does the model's performance differ across multiple languages?

- • Q3: Can domain adaptation approaches be employed to mitigate the impact of temporal concept drift on stance classification?

- • Q4: Does the semantic variation between the training and test sets lead to a degradation or an improvement of the model's predictive performance?

To this end, we (i) evaluate five publicly available monolingual and multilingual datasets, (ii) conduct a set of controlled experiments evaluating various transformer-based pretrained language models (PLMs) using chronological and random splits, and (iii) perform correlation tests to examine the relationship (i.e., positive or negative) between the model's predictive performance and the disparity between the two subsets (i.e., training and test sets).
